strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful and timely gap: combining partial observability (weakly revealing POMG/OOM machinery) with adaptive, policy-dependent adversaries under the policy regret benchmark of Arora et al. (2012).

The decoupled, non-circular formulation of the posterior-Lipschitz adversary condition via a fixed reference measure (Definition 2.2, Assumption 2.3, Remark 2.4, Appendix H.1) is a clean modeling contribution, and the critique of the circularity in the concurrent formulation is technically substantive.

The one-policy-per-epoch design is a genuine algorithmic insight: the paper quantitatively shows (Remark C.5, Appendix H.2-H.3) why flat batching with O(√T) batches forces a T^{3/4}-scale transport contribution, while geometric epochs keep it O(H² log T), preserving √T.

The causal decomposition theorem (Theorem 2.7, Appendix B) is carefully proved, with explicit attention to type-compatibility, causal timing, non-negativity, and the distinction between exact full-history factorization and κ-window reductions.

A matching Ω(√(d_E T)) lower bound, plus useful extensions (horizon adaptivity via prefix-stable confidence sets, fading-memory adversaries with an information-theoretic justification of the 1/(1−γ) cost), round out the contribution.

Limitations are treated honestly: oracle-based computation is explicitly discussed (Section 5.4), time accounting for warm-up episodes is clarified (Remark C.11), and the scope of the lower bound (no full minimax characterization of H and m) is stated plainly.
weaknesses: The hardest technical step in the new setting is assumed rather than proved: the KL-to-operator conversion (Assumption 3.1(v)) is asserted to carry over from POMDP weak-revealing analyses (Liu et al., 2022a) to the POMG setting via 'the causal decomposition', but no proof is given. Under partial observability with an adaptive adversary that marginalizes its private observations, whether the marginalized observation process retains enough revealing signal is precisely the delicate point; assuming it as an axiom weakens the central claim that the framework 'characterizes when efficient learning is possible'.

There is a potential mismatch in the lower bound: d_E = Θ(d) is claimed 'under the arm-evaluation function class', whereas the upper bound's d_E is defined through the OOM aggregate operator class F_agg (Section 2.4). That the two Eluder dimensions coincide for the ambient class M is asserted but not verified; under the tabular operator-class definition (Proposition 2.6), the dimension of the embedded instance would be much larger than d, so the claimed optimality matching is not fully established.

Substantial overlap with concurrent work (Sang & Nguyen-Tang, 2025, an ICLR submission with closely related authors and results): the posterior-Lipschitz condition, optimistic MLE approach, and overall problem are shared, and the incremental differences (epoch schedule, decoupled condition, lower bound) reduce the originality of the contribution, while the detailed T^{3/4} critique of the concurrent analysis is difficult for a reviewer to verify.

The guarantee is conditional on a long list of strong assumptions: posterior-Lipschitzness uniform over all θ ∈ Θ (Remark 2.4 admits the Lipschitz constant may be large or the class restrictive), exact warm-up stationarity (Assumption 3.1(vi)), bounded log-likelihood ratios requiring positivity/smoothing, realizability of the joint adversary-response class, and finite covering in operator norm. The resulting tabular bound (Theorem 5.3) carries H^4-scale factors, so the practical reach of the theory is limited.

The algorithm is oracle-based (MLE plus optimistic planning over a confidence set, PSPACE-hard in general), with no experiments, no posterior-sampling analysis, and no computational guarantees beyond noting planning is needed only O(log T) times.

The lower bound reduces to the standard d-armed bandit minimax bound via a memoryless adversary and fully revealing observations, so the distinctive features of the model (partial observability, adversary memory) contribute nothing to the hardness; this makes the 'minimax-optimal' framing in the title somewhat stronger than what is proven.

strengths: The problem setting is well-motivated: policy regret against adaptive adversaries in partially observable Markov games sits at a genuine gap between the policy-regret literature (Arora et al. 2012; Nguyen-Tang & Arora 2024/2025) and weakly revealing POMDP learning (Liu et al. 2022a, 2023), and no prior work fully covers this intersection.

The one-policy-per-epoch design with cumulative confidence sets is a clean and well-argued algorithmic idea. The analysis correctly identifies that the posterior-Lipschitz transport cost scales with the number of distinct deployed policies, and Appendix H.2 gives a concrete calculation showing how a flat-batching schedule with Θ(√(d_E T)) batches would yield a T^{3/4}-scale contribution via the Cauchy–Schwarz route.

The paper is transparent about scope: it explicitly states the algorithm is oracle-style with statistical (not computational) guarantees, acknowledges that the lower bound's hardness comes from bandit-like identification rather than partial observability or adversary memory, and flags the PSPACE-completeness of the planning step.

The causal decomposition (Theorem 2.7) is worked out carefully, with attention to type-compatibility via the intermediate space V, causal timing of adversary histories, and θ-independence of the aggregation operator; the appendix proof is detailed and verifiable.

The decoupled (reference-measure) formulation of the posterior-Lipschitz condition is a legitimate conceptual fix to the circularity issue identified in the concurrent work, and the paper explains why the circularity is not merely cosmetic.
weaknesses: Heavy overlap with concurrent work. The core setting, the posterior-Lipschitz adversary model, and the optimistic-MLE approach all appear in Sang & Nguyen-Tang (2025), which the paper itself identifies as 'the most closely related work.' The paper's marginal contributions reduce to (i) a decoupled Lipschitz condition, (ii) geometric epochs instead of flat batching, (iii) a bandit-style lower bound, and (iv) fading-memory/horizon adaptations. A substantial portion of the technical novelty is Appendix H, a critique of a concurrent submission whose claims cannot be fully verified from this manuscript alone.

The 'minimax-optimal' framing in the title is oversold. The lower bound (Theorem 4.1) is a direct embedding of the standard d-armed bandit bound into a fully revealing POMG with a memoryless adversary; the paper concedes that 'the hardness comes not from adversarial memory or partial observability.' Thus the lower bound matches only the √(d_E T) dependence in a degenerate instance and provides no insight into what partial observability or adaptivity actually cost.

The Eluder dimension bounds (Proposition 2.6), which are central to instantiating the main theorem for tabular, linear, and low-rank classes, are supported only by an informal proof sketch. The claim dim_E(F) = O(d_Θ log(1/ε)) via covering dimension is asserted with a citation to Russo & Van Roy (2013) that does not obviously establish it for general nonlinear operator classes; this is a technical gap in a core quantity.

Several strong assumptions are either assumed rather than proved or potentially very restrictive: Assumption 3.1(v) (KL-to-operator conversion) is imported from the POMDP setting and only asserted to extend via the causal decomposition; Assumption 2.3 requires the posterior-Lipschitz condition to hold uniformly over all θ ∈ Θ with a fixed reference measure μ_ref, which may define a very small adversary class, and the claimed examples (smoothed best response, gradient updates) are asserted but never verified; Assumption 3.1(vi) demands exact warm-up stationarity.

The horizon-adaptive claim (Section 5.1) is not reconciled with the fading-memory extension, where the warm-up length m_warmup = ⌈log(2T)/(1−γ)⌉ requires knowledge of the horizon T; the two extensions are presented in adjacent sections without addressing this tension.

The fading-memory extension silently changes the adversary model class and the estimation problem (the MLE over Φ must now handle a response depending on an internal state z_t), but the analysis does not re-examine whether likelihood-based confidence sets remain valid under this change.

Significance is modest: the upper bound follows the now-standard optimistic-MLE + Eluder template (Liu et al. 2023; Nguyen-Tang & Arora 2025), with the geometric-epoch structure as the main new ingredient. The result is a competent extension of known machinery to a new but adjacent setting, with problem-dependent factors (Hβ_T, H² log T) left unmatched.

strengths: The paper addresses a natural and well-motivated question: policy regret minimization in partially observable Markov games against adaptive adversaries, unifying the policy-regret line (Arora et al. 2012; Nguyen-Tang & Arora 2024/2025) with the weakly-revealing POMDP machinery (Liu et al. 2022a, 2023).

The core algorithmic idea is clean and well-executed: the one-policy-per-geometric-epoch structure with cumulative confidence sets keeps the posterior-Lipschitz transport term at O(H^2 log T), which is the key to recovering the sqrt(T) rate; the analysis clearly explains why flat batching with Theta(sqrt(dE T)) deployed policies would instead yield a T^{3/4}-scale contribution (Remark C.5, Appendix H.2).

The decoupled 'reference posterior-predictive' formulation (Definition 2.2) is a thoughtful fix for a genuine circularity issue in the concurrent work's posterior-Lipschitz condition, and the detailed comparison in Appendix H is technically substantive rather than merely rhetorical.

The causal decomposition theorem (Theorem 2.7) separating the world channel W_theta from the adversary aggregation operator G_{Phi,pi} is carefully constructed (Appendix B), correctly handles causal timing and type-compatibility, and is the right structural tool for disentangling world estimation from adversary-response transport.

The framework extends gracefully to horizon adaptivity (Theorem 5.1) and geometrically fading memory (Theorem 5.2), with a clean instantiation to tabular POMGs (Theorem 5.3) that reduces to known POMDP scaling when the adversary component is trivial.

The paper is honestly scoped: it explicitly flags that the results are statistical (oracle-based), that the lower bound does not close horizon/memory factors, and it includes a candid limitations discussion.
weaknesses: Heavy overlap with concurrent work: the problem setting, posterior-Lipschitz adversary class, and optimistic-MLE template are largely inherited from Sang & Nguyen-Tang (2025) and Nguyen-Tang & Arora (2024/2025); the novel delta is essentially the epoch structure, the decoupled smoothness condition, and the lower bound. This makes the contribution useful but incremental.

A central statistical ingredient is assumed rather than proved: Assumption 3.1(v) (KL-to-operator conversion) is asserted to hold for POMGs by analogy with the single-agent POMDP proof, but no POMG-specific verification is given in the appendix. Since this conversion is the engine of the entire weak-revealing argument, outsourcing it to an assumption is a significant gap.

Assumption 3.1(vi) ('exact warm-up stationarity') is very strong: it requires the m-memory adversary to be exactly at its stationary response R_inf(pi_e) for every data-collection episode, and the model itself assumes that playing a fixed policy repeatedly makes the adversary converge to a well-defined stationary R_inf(pi). Real adaptive opponents need not exhibit such exact convergence, and transient adversary dynamics during data collection would invalidate the per-epoch decomposition (23).

The lower bound is thin: it embeds the standard bandit minimax bound into a fully revealing POMG with a constant adversary, so it establishes only the sqrt(dE T) dependence in the most favorable regime; the authors acknowledge it does not characterize horizon, memory, or observability costs. As stated, the Eluder-dimension claim rests on an ambient class whose dimension is chosen to match.

The posterior-Lipschitz condition (Assumption 2.3) must hold uniformly over all theta in Theta, which is a strong requirement; and Assumption 3.1(iii) (all trajectory probabilities bounded below, via smoothing/discretization) effectively rules out large portions of the model space in a way that alters the class being analyzed.

The H beta_T factor from the stepwise KL conversion and the H^2 log T transport term make the bound visibly worse than the POMDP analogue, and the sharper aggregate KL condition that would remove the H factor (Remark C.9) is again assumed rather than established for POMGs.

No computational story: the optimistic planning step is PSPACE-hard in general, and posterior sampling is suggested only as an unproven alternative; the guarantees are oracle-flavored, limiting practical reachability.

All results are purely asymptotic theory with no experiments, which is acceptable for a theory paper but means there is no empirical evidence that the epoch-based approach behaves as the analysis predicts.

strengths: Complete theoretical treatment of a genuinely new problem combination: policy regret (counterfactual benchmark) against memory-bounded adaptive adversaries in weakly revealing POMGs. The package includes an upper bound (Theorem 3.3), a matching lower bound (Theorem 4.1), a necessity result for the statistical termination test (Proposition D.5), and extensions to unknown horizons, fading memory, and tabular instantiation.

The causal decomposition (Theorem 2.5) is a clean and useful structural result: the observable operator factors into a world channel W_theta (theta-dependent, theta-free aggregation G) with an ell_1-nonexpansive adversary aggregation. This decomposition is what enables the per-channel Eluder analysis via the channel-triangle inequalities (4) and the explicit dimension bounds in Proposition 2.6.

The algorithmic design is well-motivated and the analysis is careful: geometric epoch caps plus a data-dependent statistical termination test, with the mB_0 floor in the confidence radius that unconditionally dominates warm-up costs (Lemma D.7). The paper convincingly shows both that the test is necessary (Proposition D.5, linear regret without it) and that it fires rarely (evidence-priced terminations).

Honest and thorough treatment of concurrent work (Sang & Nguyen-Tang 2025): the paper articulates a circularity issue in the competing posterior-Lipschitz formulation and gives an explicit T^{3/4}-scale transport calculation (Appendix J) rather than vague claims, while also crediting their complementary counterexample.

Includes empirical validation that tests the paper's actual theoretical predictions (necessity of termination, sqrt(T) scaling, switch-count behavior, warm-up domination) with exact implementation of the algorithm where feasible, seeds and code provided.

Limitations are candidly discussed: computational intractability of optimistic planning (PSPACE-hardness of POMDP planning acknowledged in Section 5.4), lower bound applies in a fully revealing POMG with trivial adversary (so hardness is statistical, not from partial observability or adaptivity), and remaining gaps in H and m dependence are explicitly flagged as open.
weaknesses: The structural assumptions are strong and the burden of verification is partly shifted to the reader. Assumption 3.1(e) (KL-to-operator conversion in both joint and world-channel forms) is imposed as an assumption rather than derived in general; it is verified only for tabular classes, and its validity for linear/low-rank families (needed for Proposition 2.6 to have force there) is not carried through. Assumption 2.3 must hold uniformly over all theta in Theta, which may be restrictive for the parametric families the dimension bounds target.

The lower bound, while correct, is a direct embedding of the standard d-armed bandit construction into a fully revealing POMG with a constant adversary. It establishes minimax optimality only in the sqrt(dE T) sense; no hardness arises from partial observability or adversary adaptation, and the H and m factors in the upper bound are not matched. The 'minimax-optimal' framing in the title should be read with this caveat, which the paper does acknowledge but could emphasize more.

The statistical guarantee is decoupled from computational feasibility: optimistic planning is PSPACE-hard in general, and the termination test requires a per-episode MLE recomputation over the cumulative dataset. The practical alternative (posterior sampling) is mentioned but unanalyzed, so the contribution is statistical-only for broad classes.

The tabular dimension dE scales as H|S|^2|A||B||OA|^k |OB|^k, which grows rapidly with the weak-revealing window k and both players' observation spaces; the practical reach of the guarantee beyond small instances is limited, and the coordinate-structure hypothesis needed for linear/low-rank families explicitly rules out bilinear parameterizations.

The experiment suite is confined to bandit-embedded instances (where the MLE is closed-form) plus one simulated-adversary setup on real data; the adaptive-adversary and partial-observability aspects of the general algorithm are exercised only in the latter, smaller-scale experiment.

Presentation density: the main text introduces many objects (augmented state space, reference posterior-predictive policy, channel error classes, dyadic scales) that require substantial cross-referencing to appendices; a reader cannot fully verify the central confidence-set and termination-test mechanics from the main body alone.

strengths: The paper targets a genuinely important and underexplored problem: policy regret (rather than external regret) against m-memory-bounded adaptive adversaries in weakly revealing POMGs, which connects two previously disjoint threads (policy regret in Markov games and optimistic MLE for weakly revealing POMDPs).

The technical package is complete and coherent: a causal decomposition of the observable operator into a world channel and an adversary aggregation operator (Theorem 2.5), an epoch-based optimistic MLE algorithm with a statistical termination test, a matching Ω(√(d_E T)) lower bound, and extensions to unknown horizons and geometrically fading adversary memory.

The identification that data-dependent termination is *necessary* — Proposition D.5 shows a fixed epoch schedule provably incurs Ω(T) policy regret even in an instance satisfying all assumptions — is a sharp and valuable insight, and it is supported empirically (Experiment 1 reproduces the T/4 lower bound almost exactly).

The treatment of the concurrent work (Appendix J) is unusually detailed and constructive: the non-circular reference-measure formulation of the posterior-Lipschitz condition is a real improvement over the flat-batching formulation, and the T^{3/4}-scale transport obstruction is carefully quantified rather than asserted.

The empirical section (Appendix I) goes beyond token experiments: it verifies scaling exponents against theory (√T horizon slope 0.53, dimension slope between √d and d), tests the switch-count allowance, and includes a genuinely adaptive adversary built on real data with an honest discussion of limitations.
Limitations are discussed candidly (PSPACE-completeness of planning, per-episode MLE cost, gap √d vs d in the covering radius, open questions on H and m factors), and there are no ethical concerns.
weaknesses: The result rests on a heavy and somewhat entangled set of assumptions. Beyond the natural posterior-Lipschitz and multi-step weak-revealing conditions, Assumption 3.1(e) is imposed as an *assumption* (the KL-to-operator conversion, separately in stepwise and world-channel form) rather than derived from weak revealing in the game setting, and Assumption 3.1(c) requires uniformly bounded log-likelihood ratios achieved via smoothing/discretization, which can make B0 depend on the smoothing scale in a way that quietly degrades the bound; the paper acknowledges B0 may depend on this scale but does not quantify the cost. This bundling makes it hard to assess the true scope of the √T guarantee.

The lower bound is technically correct but does not speak to the paper's motivating difficulties: it embeds a d-armed bandit into a fully revealing (κ=1), memoryless-adversary POMG with H=2. Thus the minimax optimality claimed in the abstract is achieved only for the (√T, d_E) dependence; the horizon factor H, the memory m, and the observation-window factors |O_A|^κ|O_B|^κ that the upper bound carries are all unaccounted for, and the paper concedes no refined hard instances. The 'minimax-optimal' framing in the title is therefore stronger than what is proven.

Computational tractability is a serious practical gap. Optimistic planning is PSPACE-hard even with known parameters, the confidence-set maximization adds a further layer, and the termination test requires a full MLE re-fit after every episode. The paper is honest about this, but the guarantee is purely statistical; for a paper whose motivating examples are self-driving cars and cybersecurity, the practical relevance is limited to small tabular instances.

The Eluder-dimension bounds have noticeable looseness: the dimension scaling experiment shows fitted slope 0.78 against reference rates √d and d, and the covering-based confidence radius β_T = Θ(d) in the ambient class is loose; the paper attributes this to covering looseness, but the tabular bound still carries both |S|^2|A||B||O_A|^κ|O_B|^κ in d_E and a separate |S|(|O_A|+|O_B|) term in the radius, so the final tabular rates are far from what a reader might hope for.

Novelty is incremental in an important respect: the algorithmic skeleton (epoch-based optimistic MLE, cumulative confidence sets, Eluder summability) is inherited almost directly from Liu et al. (2023), and the policy-regret benchmark and m-memory model from Nguyen-Tang & Arora (2024/2025). The genuinely new ingredients are the causal decomposition, the termination test, and the reference-measure decoupling — real, but the paper is best viewed as a careful transfer of an existing framework to a new setting rather than a new mechanism.

The write-up is dense: the main text introduces Assumptions 2.3, 2.4, and 3.1(a)–(f) before the main theorem, with several conditions (e.g., 3.1(e) and (f)) that are analysis artifacts rather than problem features; Remark 3.2 and Appendix D cross-references do much of the load-bearing work, and a reader must jump between Sections 2–3 and Appendices D.8–D.10 to understand why the constants are what they are.

strengths: Addresses a natural and previously open question: characterizing when sublinear policy regret is achievable in partially observable Markov games against memory-bounded adaptive adversaries, unifying the weakly-revealing POMDP line (Liu et al., 2022a/2023) with the policy-regret line (Arora et al., 2012; Nguyen-Tang & Arora, 2024/2025).

The main upper bound (Theorem 3.3) achieves O~(sqrt(T)) policy regret with an explicit dependence on an aggregate Eluder dimension, and the O~(sqrt(d_E T)) rate is matched by a lower bound (Theorem 4.1), which is more than most results in this space provide.

The causal decomposition (Theorem 2.5) cleanly separates world dynamics from adversary aggregation via the B-indexed intermediate space, with the adversary operator genuinely theta-free and l1-nonexpansive; this is a real structural insight that underpins the whole analysis and is proved in full detail (Appendix B).

The epoch design with statistical termination is well motivated: Proposition D.5 proves the termination test is necessary (fixed schedules incur linear policy regret), which is a substantive algorithmic insight beyond a routine adaptation of optimistic MLE. Lemma D.7 then prices terminations in statistical evidence so warm-up costs are unconditionally dominated.

Honest and thorough treatment of limitations: computational intractability of optimistic planning (PSPACE-hardness) is discussed explicitly (Section 5.4), the lower bound's H and m dependence is acknowledged as not matched, looseness in the dimension scaling is acknowledged, and the bound's reliance on smoothing/positivity (B0) and the coordinate-structure hypothesis for linear/low-rank families is stated rather than hidden.

Empirical validation (Appendix I) is unusually strong for a theory paper: it tests the paper's three main predictions (necessity of termination, scaling rates, adaptive adversary on real digit data) with multiple seeds, confidence bands, exact algorithm implementations, and an honest scope statement; the fitted slopes (0.53, 0.35, 0.78) align well with the theory.

The comparison with concurrent work (Appendix J) is detailed and technically substantive (circularity of the posterior-Lipschitz condition, the T^{3/4} transport obstruction under flat batching), and it fairly credits the concurrent work's complementary counterexample; the decoupled reference-measure formulation (eq. 50) is a genuine modeling improvement.

The extensions (horizon-free adaptation via prefix-stable confidence analysis, fading-memory adversaries, tabular instantiation with explicit dimension counts) are natural and add value rather than being token additions.
weaknesses: The lower bound matches only the sqrt(T) and d_E dependence; the H prefactor (from the simulation lemma and the stepwise KL conversion) and the m-dependence are not matched, and the paper concedes refined hard instances are needed. The extra H in beta_bar_T = H*beta_T requires a stronger aggregate KL condition (Remark D.13) that is not established in general.

The statistical machinery leans on fairly strong assumptions: Assumption 3.1(e) (stepwise KL-to-operator conversion for both clauses) is assumed rather than always derivable, and Assumption 3.1(c) requires uniformly bounded log-likelihood increments via smoothing/discretization, which can make B0 depend on the smoothing scale in ways that are hard to quantify for a given model class.

The algorithm is oracle-based and statistically but not computationally meaningful in general; optimistic planning over confidence sets in POMGs is intractable, and the experiments only instantiate the algorithm where the MLE is closed-form. Practitioners cannot directly deploy these guarantees.

Novelty is partly compositional: the optimistic MLE framework, Eluder-dimension analysis, geometric epochs, and doubling triggers all exist in prior work (Liu et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2019; Qiao et al., 2022; Nguyen-Tang & Arora, 2025); the contribution is the careful assembly and the new structural pieces (causal decomposition, termination test necessity, lower bound) rather than an entirely new technique. Heavy overlap with the concurrent Sang & Nguyen-Tang (2025) manuscript makes it harder to fully assess independent originality, though the paper's differentiation is substantive.

The tabular bound carries the |O_A|^k |O_B|^k factor in the Eluder dimension, which is a significant cost of the adversary-side observation tracking; whether this can be avoided under information-sharing structures is left open, and the bound is consequently quite loose in some regimes.

The fading-memory extension fixes T through m_warm, weakening the horizon-free property at the same rate as the main result (the epoch-indexed warm-up restoring it is deferred to a remark); a minor inconsistency in the otherwise clean adaptivity story.

Some proofs rely on conventions stated only in appendices (dyadic grid, sign-frozen witnesses, length-matched operator supports), so a reader verifying the main text results must trace substantial detail across Appendices B-D and C; the main text is dense as a result.
